introduction: “Ye are better known to the inmates of the Kingdom on high than ye are known to your own selves.” The guide collects what was said to obscure people, many of them women and many poor, about a worth the world did not see: a station no pen can describe, a name written above, a remembrance that outlasts kings. It surrounds these assurances with the conduct that makes them credible, and with the reminder that every station is a gift. Peter called a scattering of converts a royal priesthood; Moses told Israel it was chosen though the fewest; Mary sings of the mighty put down; Paul says that God chose the weak things, and asks what anyone has that was not received. The same tradition knows the danger. Amos says “you only have I known … therefore I will punish you”; the Pharisee thanks God he is not as other men; Paul warns the grafted branch not to boast; proverb and poem (Milton’s Satan, Hamlet’s quintessence of dust) mark the two ways a high station is lost, by pride and by not believing in it.
questions: “What hast thou that thou didst not receive?” How do readings 3 and 4 shape the way all the later promises of station should be heard?
The Pharisee’s prayer and readings 54 to 58 both compare the believer with those who did not believe. What is the difference, and how is it kept?
Amos says that to be known is to be held to account, and Luke that much is required of those to whom much is given. Where in the guide does the “therefore” appear?
The woman who anointed Jesus is promised a memorial wherever the gospel is preached. What do the readings addressed to women (81 to 90, 110) claim, and against what assumptions of their time?
The Preacher’s poor wise man is forgotten. What kind of remembrance do the readings promise, and does it need anyone on earth to keep it?
Why does a guide about high station end with “well done, thou good and faithful servant” and not with a crown?

outside.why: “Ye are better known to the inmates of the Kingdom on high than ye are known to your own selves.” Paul: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
A worth unseen even by its owner. Paul to the Colossians: your life is hid with Christ in God.
Entering a city, he should become a centre of attraction by sincerity and love. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
“Serve the friends of God under all conditions.” In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.

Whatever station you reach, you recognize it as bounty and not your own capacity. What hast thou that thou didst not receive? Now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Paul’s own account of whatever he had become, after persecuting the church: by the grace of God I am what I am.
Honoured “be they rich or poor, be they captive or a prince”. Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom?
“Look not upon the loved ones of God with the eye of contempt.” Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for their angels do always behold the face of my Father.
Hebrews on the faithful who wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute and tormented: of whom the world was not worthy.
Become distinguished in all the virtues. Whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report: think on these things.
The Pen calls, and “how few” incline their ear. Many are called, but few are chosen.
If the veil were lifted and their station made manifest. The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
Through thee the eyes of the dwellers of Paradise are gladdened, and people are heedless of it. Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
A station “that neither the minds of the wise” can conceive. Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man.
A station none has understood. Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be.
These souls “are, in the sight of God, on the same plane”. The labourers of the first hour and of the eleventh receive the same penny.
Well is it with the man-servant and with the maid-servant who has attained. There is neither male nor female: for ye are all one.
The Qur’an’s long verse names them in pairs: men who surrender and women who surrender, men who believe and women who believe; for them God hath prepared forgiveness and a vast reward.
Their very breath is “richer than all the treasures of the earth”. One pearl of great price, for which a merchant sells all that he has.
“We have created you to behold Our own Beauty.” One thing have I desired: to behold the beauty of the Lord.
“From amongst all mankind hath He chosen you.” Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, called out of darkness into his marvellous light.
Moses tells Israel why: not because ye were more in number than any people, for ye were the fewest; but because the Lord loved you.

Amos draws the other consequence of being chosen: you only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities. Which of the readings carry that “therefore”?
Divines and theologians remained veiled “while thou … attained”. Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
Princes erased from the scroll and the lowly written in. He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
“Most of the divines, mystics and princes remained deprived.” The Pharisees take that for an argument: have any of the rulers believed on him? But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed.

The Pharisee in the temple thanks God that he is not as other men are. A believer who is told “they set while you rose” stands near that prayer. What in the readings keeps the comparison from becoming his?
The nobles took the path of nothingness. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Thou turnedst when the scholars turned away. Paul to Gentile converts pleased with themselves: boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.
“Thou art he who heard the Call and responded.” Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth.
The turning away of the peoples did not prevent this soul. Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, and few there be that find it.
The glory of being a handmaiden at the threshold. Mary, calling herself the handmaiden of the Lord: my soul doth magnify the Lord.
Arise to fulfil the conditions of servitude and be a sign. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
“It befits you to glory and boast over the queens.” Jeremiah allows one boast: let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.

Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall; better to be of an humble spirit with the lowly. The reading uses the language of boasting to console the lowly. When does consolation become the pride the proverb warns of?
Outwardly lowly in the eyes of the proud. Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
How many men are veiled, and how many women have attained. The first to see the risen Jesus, in John, is Mary Magdalene.
Women have been raised up who are each a mighty sign. Deborah’s song of the day a woman led Israel: the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.
Mill argued in 1869 that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself, and one of the chief hindrances to human improvement.
Every maidservant who arises will become a star of guidance. Philip had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.
Her influence continues to spread. Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.
Though “seated on the dust”, in the eyes of God on seats of honour. James rebukes the congregation that tells the poor man: sit here under my footstool.
Faith requires “the station of sacrifice”. Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God.
A high station is a demand as well as a gift. Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
“Ye will, with your own eyes, witness how brilliantly every one of you” will shine. Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun.

“Ye are the breezes of spring.” Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? The Gospel’s praise of the disciple carries its condition in the same breath. Where do these readings state theirs?
Though they live on earth, they are heavenly. Our conversation is in heaven.
Their ideals soar above this age. Jesus prays not that his friends be taken out of the world, but that they be kept from the evil. How does one benefit humanity from above it?
“They write upon the surface of iron and steel.” Oh that my words were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever!
They become “radiant stars in the horizon of eternal glory”. They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.
His remembrance may shine through eternity. The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
The Preacher saw a poor wise man deliver a city; yet no man remembered that same poor man. The readings promise a remembrance the world does not keep. Where is it kept?
The station of one whose will has become “extinct in His Will”. Dante’s Piccarda, in the lowest sphere of heaven and content: in His will is our peace.
Blessed is he who is content with all that has come from God. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Those whom rejection does not deter. Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life.
“Grieve thou not over anything.” If God be for us, who can be against us?
Be among those who have no fear. Fear thou not; for I am with thee.
“Kings will seek blessing from his dust.” Kings shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet.
“Do something so you never die.” Whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.
The prison became “the glory and pride of souls”. At midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
Lovelace from the Gatehouse prison: stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
“Know thou thy station.” Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
Hamlet recites the same dignity, noble in reason, in apprehension how like a god, and ends: what is this quintessence of dust? What does a station feel like to someone who cannot feel it?
“In this we take pride.” He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.
Mentioned among the inhabitants of Paradise in the Book of Names. To him that overcometh will I give a white stone, and in the stone a new name written.
“You are the friends of the Ancient Beauty.” Henceforth I call you not servants, but I have called you friends.
Counted “among those few souls”. Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
Bearers of a great trust. Keep that which is committed to thy trust.
Milton’s Satan would rather reign in hell than serve in heaven. Every promise of rank in this guide is made to servants. Why does the guide’s title join dignity to service?
Thanks for having been enabled to serve. Well done, thou good and faithful servant.

shortfall: Many of the readings are short assurances to individuals that repeat a single thought (a station beyond description, blessed art thou for having attained); a companion was given to each form of the thought and not to each letter.
